newsitem.title: BRAZIL: AMR Brazil airline deal boon for both.
newsitem.headline: AMR Brazil airline deal boon for both.

text.p: An accord between American Airlines and Brazil's TAM will boost the U.S. firm's presence in the rapidly growing Latin American market and help TAM offer flight to the United States, officials said.
American Airlines chief Robert Crandall said a code- sharing agreement signed Tuesday with TAM will help the U.S. carrier form a regional network.
"The airline business nowadays is to form a network. Passengers prefer to travel under a single code," Crandall said.

The accord, the latest in a series involving Brazil, gives American a new weapon to beat competition from United Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines. Airlines also signed a code-sharing deal, while Delta and Continental have announced daily flights to Brazil.
The latest partnership, which takes effect on August 1, will allow passengers to swap tickets and reservations and benefit from frequent-flier mileage programs offered by both companies.

According to TAM President Rolim Adolfo Amaro, the company will benefit from American Airlines' expertise in offering international flights and also take advantage of American's facilities in the U.S.
Rolim said revenue from the deal is likely to reach 35 percent of the company's total sales by 2000 and increase number of passengers transported per year by one million.

TAM, the fatest growing carrier in Latin America, with revenues of $580 million in 1996, currently carries four million passengers a year. It specializes in offering business flights in Brazil and to the Mercosur trade bloc comprised of Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina and Brazil.

TAM recently announced it would offer daily flights to Miami within 12 months and plans to lease at least two aircraft to start this service. Rolim added TAM would spend about $100 million per aircraft to lease the same the Boeing, Airbus and other aircraft used by American Airlines. TAM now operates mostly Fokkers.
The accord also allows the companies to use each other's aircraft in the U.S. or Brazil when they are not being used by the owner.
"This will lower the per hour cost (of operating an aircraft) because it will be flying more," said Luiz Carlos Falco, TAM's vice president said.

Currently, TAM has a fleet of 30 Fokker-100s, nine Fokker F-50s, 38 Caravans, as well as 22 small craft and helicopters. American Airlines fleet consists of 643 aircraft, including Airbuses, Boeings and Fokkers.
